To Critic Or Not To Critic

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (233 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.32013v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As large language models tackle longer and more complex tasks, understanding when a critic improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes increasingly vital. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains a critic to reduce variance and provide fine-grained credit assignment, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) drops the critic and avoids the bias of bootstrapping from the critic's value estimates. Although recent critic-based methods have reported strong performance relative to GRPO, it remains unclear when each approach is preferable. We argue that there is no universal answer; instead, the choice depends on several interacting factors, including batch size, critic reliance, and task complexity. We study the bias-variance tradeoff in terms of gradient direction, measuring how closely each method's gradient estimates align with the true policy gradient as batch size grows. Under a shared actor objective, we compare GRPO with PPO in control tasks, short-horizon math, and long-horizon terminal agents. Across more than 1,200 training runs, including 96 with LLMs, we find that PPO generally leads at small batch sizes, while GRPO often overtakes heavily bootstrapped PPO and reaches parity with lightly bootstrapped PPO at larger batches. At longer horizons and in more complex domains, GRPO needs larger batches to catch up to PPO's performance. Accounting for training compute, critics pay off at small budgets, but their returns diminish at larger budgets.

arXiv:2611.32009v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention: tasks should continue between interactions, and users should be able to return with little effort to understand and control them. We develop this position as Calm Agent. It connects three on-demand interaction modes: Delegate, Adjust, and Check, through a persistent task representation. Generative interaction provides controls and feedback suited to open-ended goals, while existing controls support routine actions. We illustrate these principles with Orvlet, a desktop prototype for background execution and compact task interfaces. We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Latent world models learn compact recurrent dynamics from offline trajectories, yet deployed simulators can retain backdoor triggers or stale transitions from outdated physical regimes. Existing unlearning methods fail in autoregressive physics: gradient updates distort latent manifolds and compound rollout drift, naive output zeroing suppresses valid control responses on trigger onset, and single-step deletion leaves corruption inside recurrent hidden states. We propose Analytical Dynamics Excision (ADE), a deterministic, zero-training closed-form unlearning algorithm for latent world models. Using only cached pretraining moments, ADE recovers retain covariances via single-pass matrix downdating without raw retain data and cascades closed-form edits across the input bottleneck, hidden states, and downstream heads. Pairing orthogonal excision with whitened recurrent damping and mean-preserving affine calibration neutralizes out-of-manifold backdoors and realigns in-manifold shifts without variance collapse. Across four regimes on three MuJoCo benchmarks, ADE outperforms seven tuned baselines on DreamerV1, eliminating HalfCheetah and Hopper velocity-flip triggers $4.4\times$ faster than fine-tuning, and transfers zero-shot to DreamerV3.

We put four questions to a mid-size open model, on recurrent networks of 1{,}218 weights with exactly checkable answers. Given a population of opponents described in English, write a policy that is optimal: its value is a finite computation over the agent's information state, so a submitted network has an exact gap from the optimum. Given a network's weights, report its action after each of fifteen opponent histories; recover the state machine it implements, judged on every opponent sequence to depth ten; or repair a network whose output was altered in one place and say which round first goes wrong. Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (230 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.31977v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.

Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (245 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.31962v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31950v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hands grasp objects with soft skin. A fingertip flattens against a mug, and a palm curves around a bottle. Yet hand-object datasets and estimators represent the hand as a rigid articulated mesh, which hovers above or penetrates the object where skin would press against it. Existing refiners keep the mesh rigid and adjust only the pose, trading pose accuracy for physical plausibility. We ask whether a rigid hand can instead touch the object as skin does while staying close to its original pose. We lift annotated or estimated rigid hands to contact-consistent meshes through an optimization that (i) slightly adjusts the joints and wrist to bring the fingers onto the object, (ii) deforms the skin so that penetrating regions settle onto the surface, and (iii) keeps this deformation consistent over time. Since deformation reaches only skin already near the object, we further train a lightweight head on the lifted annotations to predict where an estimated hand should touch and steer the deformation there. Unlike existing refiners, the lift more than doubles the skin lying on the object surface for three published estimators while barely changing the pose. Guidance from the learned head further improves grasp stability by closing contact gaps that the estimate leaves open. Existing hand-object datasets and estimators can thus adopt contact-consistent hands without changing the hand model or retraining the estimators.

arXiv:2611.31909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models (VLMs): even when their coordinate predictions are incorrect, they can describe visual evidence worth inspecting. We introduce \textbf{SPARK}, \textit{\textbf{S}emantic \textbf{P}robe-guided \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{R}egion see\textbf{K}ing}, a training-free framework that turns this semantic guidance into targeted visual observations. Exploration probes describe relevant context and distinguishing target details, while verification probes identify evidence needed to assess emerging hypotheses. Their spatial attention guides view placement, contextual responses determine crop extent, and observation history encourages complementary inspection. The resulting predictions are combined through uncertainty-weighted voting. On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and UI-TARS, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Consistent gains across four additional benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse interfaces and grounding tasks. These results establish semantic probing as an effective mechanism for turning a frozen VLM's understanding of what to inspect into more accurate GUI grounding.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31902v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Flow-based policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. In online actor-critic learning, off-policy value estimates can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, where expressive policies may shift probability mass toward critic-favored actions. We propose MIFLOW, which calibrates online flow-policy learning with a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions. Inspired by canalization as a qualitative analogy for path-dependent stabilization, we use the prior as a moving density reference for value-guided policy improvement. MIFLOW uses the approximate recent-action log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets. This correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, MIFLOW achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks. In a Walker2d-v4 case study, MIFLOW shows a lower proportion of actions assigned low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. Prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and prior-defined diagnostics. These results support dynamic recent-behavior priors for reference calibration in the evaluated settings. The diagnostics measure how sampled actions align with the learned reference. True action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured in these experiments.

arXiv:2611.31895v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video understanding depends not only on how models reason about visual evidence, but also on which evidence they observe. Fixed observation policies determine this evidence in advance; agentic harnesses allow models to seek further observations as their understanding develops. This shift creates an opportunity to realize capabilities that fixed inputs leave untapped, yet the ability to request observations does not ensure their effective use. We investigate when and why video harnesses improve understanding, examining how task demands and models' capacity for interaction jointly shape their benefits. Using Video-Relook as an experimental framework, we let models adapt their temporal and spatial observations from a common default configuration, and analyze performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks. Adaptive observation yields substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2. Even under the same observation interface, gains differ substantially across models; interaction traces reveal corresponding differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision. The benefits also vary across tasks for the same model, ranging from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions. Together, these findings support an account in which harness effectiveness depends on the alignment between opportunities for informative observation and the model's ability to turn interaction into reliable revisions. They motivate video harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning, matching observational autonomy to task demands and model capabilities.

CALVIN-MAX: When Does a Mid-Execution Change Hurt a Robot Policy?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (300 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.31868v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robots must often keep working after the world changes, as when a block moves or the camera shifts while the robot still acts on what it saw before. Recent work demonstrated that one change during a task lowers success for every policy tested, but did not separate the effect of its timing from the cost of the changed world, or measure what it costs afterwards. We introduce CALVIN-MAX, a benchmark of 7,828 cases on CALVIN's five-instruction chains, each with one change to the objects, the camera, the robot, or the instruction. Each case compares three runs that are identical until the affected instruction begins: one without the change, one with it in place from that moment, and one in which it arrives while the robot is moving. The second run against the first gives the cost of the changed world, and the third against the second the effect of meeting it mid-motion. On 1,526 held-out cases per policy, with hypotheses fixed in advance, each of ten released policies loses 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction over the eight core changes. Whether timing matters depends on the change: one that alters what the robot sees costs 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start, whereas a change to the scene itself or to the robot indicates no detectable effect. Rewinding the robot to the start of the instruction removes the benefit for every policy; the stricter test we fixed in advance, that the rewound run then matches the second run, passes for three. The cost also outlasts the affected instruction: the change stays in place, and a policy that still completes that instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31850v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale pretraining provides embodied models with general capabilities, but reliable task execution still requires post training. In multitask settings, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) faces distribution mismatch between training and deployment, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) is limited by sparse rewards and uneven learning progress across tasks. Multi-teacher on policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates expert capabilities through dense supervision on the model's own trajectories, but achieving performance beyond the teachers remains challenging. We propose a two-stage post training framework for flow-based embodied models, constructing distillation objectives from the velocity regression formulation of conditional flow matching. Stage 1 efficiently consolidates expert capabilities through MOPD. Stage 2 combines RL with teacher distillation that weights velocity errors according to the sampling noise, where distillation is restricted to failed trajectories to supplement sparse rewards with dense guidance without directly constraining successful behaviors. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that the framework outperforms joint SFT and exceeds the corresponding teachers' aggregate success rates. Sample efficiency comparisons show higher success rates than direct RL with fewer environment interactions.

JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (238 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.

arXiv:2611.31848v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard LLM personalization typically frames identity as a static retrieval task, overlooking the inherent incongruity of human personas, where stable traits coexist with atypical, context-specific stances. Existing methods struggle to reconcile these dimensions: prompting succumbs to context drift over long sequences, while fine-tuning often suppresses idiosyncratic "quirks" in favor of generic distributional patterns. To bridge this gap, we present QuirkyMind, a framework that disentangles identity definition from its expression. First, Traits Anchoring constructs a dual-stream latent state, fusing a sentence-level summary for semantic stability with a token-level sequence for generative control. This state is stabilized via In-Context Narrative Refinement using an alternating objective: a discriminative InfoNCE loss anchors the persona in representation space to prevent drift, while a generative cross-entropy loss ensures faithful verbalization. Finally, Persona Steered Generalization transfers the refined state to downstream tasks via parameter-efficient adapters. Empirical evaluations on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference demonstrate that QuirkyMind mitigates drift, consolidating persona knowledge without erasing authentic incongruities.

arXiv:2611.31839v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: SWE-bench-style benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Verified (Verified) and SWE-bench Pro (Pro), evaluate coding agents with tests taken from the change that originally fixed each issue. However, these tests can enforce details the task never states, causing correct alternative fixes to fail. Such overspecified tests have so far been found mainly through expensive expert review. To address this, we define the Spec-Test Coverage Gap (STCG), a 1-4 scale measuring overspecification, and score it with two LLM judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, which are given the specification and the test patch. A task is flagged as overspecified when both judges score it 3 or higher. Our study has three parts. First, we validate the judges on 206 tasks that earlier human audits and agent results label as overspecified or fine. Second, we apply STCG to all 500 Verified and 731 public Pro tasks and compare the flags with the results of the top 30 Verified submissions. Third, we verify the flags by asking Claude Opus 5.5 to loosen the overspecified requirements of flagged tasks, and regrade 2,186 failed patches from those submissions. Our main findings are: (1) Overspecified tests are detectable: on the validation tasks, the judges correctly flag 89% of the tasks that human audits identify as overspecified and wrongly flag only 4% of the tasks known to be fine. (2) Overspecified tests are common: applied to whole benchmarks, the judges flag 23% of Verified and 35% of Pro tasks. (3) Flagged tasks are much harder for agents: the top 30 Verified submissions resolve only 31% of the flagged tasks on average, against 88% of the other tasks. (4) Overspecified tests change the leaderboard: relaxing the tests lets 61% of the 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass. Counting these patches as resolved would add 33 to 60 tasks to each top-30 submission, raising resolve rates by up to 12 percentage points.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.31836v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Where a person looks indicates their focus of attention, and how their gaze shifts between targets reveals how that attention responds to a changing scene. Existing gaze target estimation methods largely operate frame by frame and do not model these shifts. Gaze shifts are often driven by dynamic changes in the scene, which is the kind of information world models are designed to encode. This relationship is subtle, however, since an event far across the frame may produce only a slight movement of the person's head or eyes. We therefore introduce the Gaze World Model (GWM), which co-trains latent scene prediction with person-conditioned gaze supervision on a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; in our ablations, the latent prediction objective improves both shift detection and gaze localization. Given a video clip and the person's head box, GWM estimates gaze locations and detects gaze shifts in the observed clip, and forecasts future gaze and shifts from predicted scene features. To train and evaluate these tasks, we augment VideoAttentionTarget and ChildPlay with event-level gaze-shift annotations. GWM achieves state-of-the-art shift detection on these benchmarks, about 10 points higher in four-class AP than the strongest baseline, while remaining comparable to the strongest image-based models in gaze target estimation, and outperforms the compared baselines on future gaze localization and shift forecasting.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.31835v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Actor-critic methods achieve high returns in robotic control, yet trained actors exhibit high-frequency action oscillations. Most smoothness methods constrain the actor, whereas PAVE regularizes the critic by separately penalizing action-gradient variation and encouraging negative action curvature. The same gradient change, however, moves the critic's preferred action farther where the critic is flat, and separate penalties do not measure this motion. We characterize this motion through the greedy shift, which approximates greedy-action displacement across state transitions to first order under local concavity. Since displacement alone does not reflect its critic-value consequences, the analysis further highlights that the shift's curvature-weighted energy approximates the value lost by retaining the previous greedy action to second order. Based on this relationship, POISE regularizes the curvature-weighted energy along temporal and spatial state displacements. It employs a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling while leaving the actor unchanged. On six continuous control tasks with TD3, POISE reduces the smoothness score on every task by $5.9\times$ on average ($4.5\times$ geometric mean), compared with $2.2\times$ ($1.9\times$) for the strongest baseline, and achieves the lowest score on five tasks. Paired return intervals include zero on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.

arXiv:2611.31821v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The training of socially intelligent language models often relies on large language model (LLM) judges, which are expensive, noisy, and vulnerable to reward hacking. Multi-player social games offer a natural alternative: they require open-ended communication to coordinate with teammates and infer hidden roles, while their rules provide an objective outcome which can serve as a verifiable reward for training. Using three social games, we explore how much social intelligence Qwen3 models can acquire through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Results show that against a much stronger Gemma-3-27B model, SFT and RLVR raise the win rate of Qwen3-4B from 33% to 81% on the three trained games, and from 39% to 54% on three additional held-out games. In contrast, in-context strategies such as prompting improve the win rate of Qwen3-4B by only about 6 pp across the same games we train and evaluate on. Furthermore, we show that the gains from SFT and RLVR hold across the model sizes 1.7B, 4B, and 32B. Qualitative analyses of agent behavior show signs of stronger social intelligence; for example, trained agents tend to share information more openly, check each other's claims against public evidence, and coordinate their votes. More broadly, our results demonstrate that training LLMs on verifiable outcomes in social games can cultivate generalizable social behaviors, which offers a scalable path for building socially intelligent agents.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31813v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it. We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost. We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.

How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (287 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.31801v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.

arXiv:2611.31800v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.

Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. VISOR consists of two components: 1) a text-free stochastic predictor that samples diverse candidate futures, and 2) a VLM selector that reads the candidates as a single chart image and selects one based on the text. To avoid overly calm forecasting paths, we train the selector with a shape-aware target that evaluates each candidate based on both point-wise error and path shape. Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31771v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic retrieval struggles with multi-hop question answering on both recall and precision: gold passages are buried among distractors that degrade the reader's answer, and retrieving them requires reasoning over the query rather than matching it. GraphRAG techniques expand semantic retrieval by connecting passages to graph nodes and performing one or more hops of expansion after initial retrieval. This improves recall, but multi-hop expansion becomes expensive and brings additional noise into the retrieved set. We break this tradeoff by \emph{interleaving} dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal for complex multi-hop questions. Dense retrieval locates the first relevant regions of the search space at good recall, while traversal of a pre-existing external KG (Wikidata) restores precision and improves recall by confirming retrieved passages against a reasoning path through the KG. To keep traversal both question-adaptive and reliable, we have an LLM plan it as code generation task for graph traversal in SPARQL format but \emph{parse rather than execute} the query. On full 1{,}000-question splits under a shared corpus and reader, and with a single configuration applied identically to every dataset, we reach \textbf{62.5 / 75.1} EM/F1 on HotpotQA, \textbf{73.5 / 81.0} on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and \textbf{37.1 / 50.0} on MuSiQue, ahead of reproduced HippoRAG2, T\textsuperscript{2}RAG, and IRCoT on all three benchmarks. A second, token-matched setting stays ahead of T\textsuperscript{2}RAG on HotpotQA and 2Wiki while spending roughly its per-query budget. Executing the generated SPARQL instead of parsing it costs up to 11.4 EM, mostly because raw queries return empty results, not because of syntax errors.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.

#9130. Latest Update: Optimization story: Bloom inference

📅 12 Oct 2022 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3488 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Optimization story: Bloom inference

📅 12 Oct 2022 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article gives you the behind-the-scenes of how we made an efficient inference server that powers bloom.
  • Recent findings suggest that we achieved a 5x latency reduction over several weeks (and 50x more throughput).
  • It has been revealed that A lot of different people were involved at many stages so not everything will be covered here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article gives you the behind-the-scenes of how we made an efficient inference server that powers bloom. inference server that powers https://huggingface.co/bigscience/bloom.

Recent findings suggest that we achieved a 5x latency reduction over several weeks (and 50x more throughput). We wanted to share all the struggles and epic wins we went through to achieve such speed improvements.

It has been revealed that A lot of different people were involved at many stages so not everything will be covered here. And please bear with us, some of the content might be outdated or flat out wrong because we're still learning how to optimize extremely large models and lots of new hardware features and content keep coming out regularly.

If your favorite flavor of optimizations is not discussed or improperly represented, we're sorry, please share it with us we're more than happy to try out newly introduced stuff and correct our mistakes.

This goes without saying but without the large model being accessible in the first place, there would be no real reasons to optimize inference for it. This was an incredible effort led by many different people.

Industry observers note that to maximize the GPU during training, several solutions were explored and in the end, Megatron-Deepspeed was chosen to train the end model. This meant that the code as-is wasn't necessarily compatible with the transformers library.

Because of the original training code, we set out to do something which we regularly do: port an existing model to transformers. The goal was to extract from the training code the relevant parts and implement it within transformers. This effort was tackled by Younes. This is by no means a small effort as it took almost a month and 200 commits to get there.

There are several things to note that will come back later:.

We needed to have smaller models bigscience/bigscience-small-testing and bigscience/bloom-560m. This is extremely important because they are smaller, so everything is faster when working with them.

First, you have to abandon all hope to have exactly the same logits at the end down to the bytes. PyTorch versions can change the kernels and introduce subtle differences, and different hardware might yield different results because of different architecture (and you probably don't want to develop on a A100 GPU all the time for cost reasons).

Getting a good strict test suite is really important for all models.

The best test we found was having a fixed set of prompts. You know the prompt, you know the completion that needs to be deterministic so greedy. If two generations are identical, you can basically ignore small logits differences Whenever you see a drift, you need to investigate. It could be that your code is not doing what it should OR that you are actually out of domain for that model and therefore the model is more sensitive to noise. If you have several prompts and long enough prompts, you're less likely to trigger that for all prompts by accident. The more prompts the better, the longer the better.

Recent findings suggest that the first model (small-testing) is in bfloat16 like the big bloom so everything should be very similar, but it wasn't trained a lot or just doesn't perform well, so it highly fluctuates in outputs. That means we had issues with those generation tests. The second model is more stable but was trained and saved in float16 instead of bfloat16. That's more room for error between the two.

To be perfectly fair bfloat16 -> float16 conversion seemed to be OK in inference mode (bfloat16 mostly exists to handle large gradients, which do not exist in inference).

It has been revealed that during that step, one important tradeoff was discovered and implemented. Because bloom was trained in a distributed setting, part of the code was doing Tensor parallelism on a Linear layer meaning running the same operation as a single operation on a single GPU was giving different results. This took a while to pinpoint and either we went for 100% compliance and the model was much slower, or we would take a small difference in generation but was much faster to run and simpler code. We opted for a configurable flag.

Now we have a workable transformers clean version of the start working on running this.

Bloom is a 352GB (176B parameters in bf16) model, we need at least that much GPU RAM to make it fit. We briefly explored offloading to CPU on smaller machines but the inference speed was orders of magnitude slower so we discarded it.

According to recent reports, then we wanted to basically use the pipeline. So it's dogfooding and this is what the API uses under the hood all the time.

Sources indicate that however pipelines are not distributed aware (it's not their goal). After briefly discussing options, we ended up using accelerate newly created device_map="auto" to manage the sharding of the model. We had to iron out a few bugs, and fix the transformers code a bit to help accelerate do the right job.

It works by splitting the various layers of the transformers and giving part of the model to each GPU. So GPU0 gets to work, then hands it over to GPU1 so on and so forth.

In the end, with a small HTTP server on top, we could start serving bloom (the significant model) !!

But we haven't even started discussing optimizations yet!

We actually have quite a bit, all this process is a castle of cards. During optimizations we are going to make modifications to the underlying code, being extra sure you're not killing the model in one way or the other is really notable and easier to do than you think.

Recent findings suggest that so we are now at the very first step of optimizations and we need to start measuring and keep measuring performance. So we need to consider what we care about. For an open inference server supporting many options, we expect customers to send many queries with different parameters and what we care about are:.

The number of consumers we can serve at the same time (throughput) How long does it take for an average user to be served (latency)?

We made a testing script in locust which is exactly this:.

**Note: This is not the best nor the only load testing we used, but it was always the first to be run so that it could compare fairly across approaches. Being the best on this benchmark does NOT mean it is the best solution. Other more complex scenarios had to be used in addition to actual real-world performance. **.

Industry observers note that we wanted to observe the ramp-up for various implementations and also make sure that underload the server properly circuit breaked. Circuit breaking means that the server can answer (fast) that it will not answer your query because too many people are trying to use it at the same time. It's extremely important to avoid the hug of death.

On this benchmark the initial performance was (on 16xA100 40Go on GCP which is the machine used throughout):.

Requests/s : 0.3 (throughput) Latency: 350ms/token (latency).

Those numbers are not that great. Before getting to work let's estimate the best we can imagine achieving. The formula for amount of operations is 24Bsh^2 + 4𝐵s^2h24Bsh^2 + 4𝐵s^2h where B is the batch size, s the sequence length, and h the hidden dimension.

Let's do the math and we are getting 17 TFlop for a single forward pass. Looking at the specs of A100 it claims 312 TFLOPS for a single card. That means a single GPU could potentially run at 17 / 312 = 54ms/token. We're using 16 of those so 3ms/token on the overall machine. Take all these numbers with a big grain of salt, it's never possible to reach those numbers, and real-life performance rarely matches the specs. Also if computation is not your limiting factor then this is not the lowest you can get. It's just good practice to know how far you are from your target. In this case, we're 2 orders of magnitude so pretty far. Also, this estimate puts all the flops at the service of latency which means only a single request can go at a time (it's ok since you're maximizing your machine so there's not much else to be done, but we can have higher latency and get throughput back through batching much more easily).

Now that we have a good understanding of where we stand it's time to get to work.

We tried many different things based on the people and our various knowledge.

Sources indicate that ALL endeavors deserve their own blog post so I'll just list them, explain the few final learnings and delve into the details of only what went into the current server. Moving from Pipeline Parallelism (PP) to Tensor Parallelism (TP) is one substantial interesting change for latency. Each GPU will own part of the parameters and all will be working at the same time. So the latency should decrease drastically but the price to pay is the communication overhead since they regularly need to communicate with each other about their results.

It is to note that this is a very wide range of approaches and the intent was deliberately to learn more about each tool and how it could fit in later endeavors.

The first item on the list was removing unnecessary operations in the first implementations Some can be seen by just looking at the code and figuring out obvious flaws:.

The old code: link The newly introduced code: link.

Sources indicate that this is a 10x speedup and the latest version includes padding too! Since this step is only computed once, the actual speed is not key but overall reducing the number of operations and tensor creation is a good direction.

Other parts come out more clearly when you start profiling and we used quite extensively the tensorboard extension.

This provides this sort of image which give insights:.

According to recent reports, removing a lot of reshape/transpose, for instance, we figured out that: - The attention is the hot path (it's expected but always good to verify). - In the attention, a lot of kernels were actual copies due to the massive amount of reshapes - We could remove the reshapes by reworking the weights themselves and the past. This is a breaking change but it did improve performance quite a bit!

In a recent development, ok, we have removed most of the low-hanging fruits now we went roughly from 350ms/token latency to 300ms/token in PP. That's a 15% reduction in latency, but it actually provided more than that, but we were not extremely rigorous in our measuring initially so let's stick to that figure.

Then we went on to provide a TP implementation. Turned out to be much faster than we anticipated the implementation took half a day of a single (experienced) dev. The result is here. We were also able to reuse code from other projects which helped.

The latency went directly from 300ms/token to 91ms/token which is a huge improvement in user experience. A simple 20 tokens request went from 6s to 2s which went from a "slow" experience to slightly delayed.

Also, the throughput went up a lot to 10RPS. The throughput comes from the fact that running a query in batch_size=1 takes the same time as batch_size=32 and throughput becomes essentially free in latency cost at this point.

Recent findings suggest that now that we had a TP implementation, we could start profiling and optimizing again. It's a significant enough shift that we had to start from scratch again.

According to recent reports, the first thing that stood out, is that synchronization (ncclAllReduce) starts to become a preponderant part of the load, which is expected, this is the synchronization part and it is taking some time. We never tried to look and optimize this as it's already using nccl but there might still be some room for improvement there. We assumed it would be hard to do much better.

The second thing is that Gelu operator was launching many elementwise kernels and overall it was taking a bigger share of compute than we expected.

This transforms the operations from multiple small element-wise kernels (and hence tensor copies) to a single kernel operation!

This provided a 10% latency improvement from 91ms/token to 81ms/token, right there!

Be careful though, this is not some magic black box you can just throw everywhere, the kernel fusion will not necessarily happen or the previously used operations are already extremely efficient.

Places where we found it worked well:.

We also had some points, during our testing periods, where we ended up seeing some consistent 25% lower latency for the Rust server compared to the Python one. This was rather odd, but because it was consistently measured, and because removing kernels provided a speed up, we were under the impression that maybe dropping the Python overhead could provide a nice boost.

Sources indicate that we started a 3-day job to reimplement the necessary parts of torch.distributed To get up and running in the Rust world nccl-rs. We had the version working but something was off in the generations compared to its Python counterpart. During the investigation of the complications, we figured... that we had forgotten to remove the profiler in the Pytorch measurements...

That was the epic fail because removing it gave us back the 25% and then both codes ran just as fast. This is what we initially expected, that python mustn't be a performance hit, since it's mostly running torch cpp's code. In the end, 3 days is not the end of the world, and it might become useful sometime in the future but still pretty bad. This is quite common when doing optimizations to do wrong or misrepresentative measurements which end up being disappointing or even detrimental to the overall product. This is why doing it in small steps and having expectations about the outcome as soon as possible helps contain that risk.

Sources indicate that another place where we had to be extra careful, was the initial forward pass (without past) and the later forward passes (with past). If you optimize the first one, you're most certainly going to be slowing down the later ones which are much more important and account for most of the runtime. Another pretty common culprit is measuring times which are CPU times, and not actual CUDA times, so you need to torch.cuda.synchronize() when doing runs to be sure that the kernels complete.

So far, we had achieved close to DeepSpeed performance without any custom code outside of PyTorch! Pretty neat. We also didn't have to make any compromise on the flexibility of the run time batch size!

But given the DeepSpeed experience, we wanted to try and write a custom kernel to fuse a few operations in the hot path where torch.jit.script wasn't able to do it for us. Essentially the following two lines:.

The first masked fill is creating a new tensor, which is here only to say to the softmax operator to ignore those values. Also, the softmax needs to be calculated on float32 (for stability) but within a custom kernel, we could limit the amount of upcasting necessary so we limit them to the actual sums and accumulated needed.

Code can be found here. Keep in mind we had a single GPU architecture to target so we could focus on this and we are not experts (yet) at writing kernels, so there could be better ways to do this.

It has been revealed that this custom kernel provided yet another 10% latency increase moving down from 81ms/token to 71ms/token latency. All the while keeping our flexibility.

Recent findings suggest that after that, we investigated and explored other things like fusing more operators removing other reshapes, or putting them in other places. But no attempt ever made a significant enough impact to make it to the final versions.

Industry observers note that just like the Rust counterpart, we had to implement the batching of requests with different parameters. Since we were in the PyTorch world, we have pretty much full control of what's going on. Since we're in Python, we have the limiting factor that the torch.distributed needs to run on several processes instead of threads, which means it's slightly harder to communicate between processes. In the end, we opted to communicate raw strings over a Redis pub/sub to distribute the requests to all processes at once. Since we are in different processes it's easier to do it that way than communicating tensors (which are way bigger) for instance.

Then we had to drop the use generate since this applies the parameters to all members of the batch, and we actually want to apply a different set of parameters. Thankfully, we can reuse lower-level items like the LogitsProcessor to save us a lot of work.

So we reconstructed a generate function that takes a list of parameters and applies them to each member of the batch.

Another really important aspect of the final UX is latency. Since we have different parameter sets for different requests, we might have.

In a recent development, 1 request for 20 tokens and the other for 250 tokens. Since it takes 75ms/token latency one request takes 1.5s and the other 18s. If we were batching all the way, we would be making the user that asked to wait for 18s and making it appear to him as if we were running at 900ms/token which is quite slow!

It has been revealed that since we're in a PyTorch world with extreme flexibility, what we can do instead is extract from the batch the first request as soon as we generated to first 20 tokens, and return to that user within the requested 1.5s! We also happen to save 230 tokens worth of computation.

So flexibility is notable to get the best possible latency out there.

Sources indicate that optimization is a never-ending job, and like any other project, 20% of work will usually yield 80% of the results. At some point, we started having a small testing strategy to figure out potential yields of some idea we had, and if the tests didn't yield significant results then we discarded the idea. 1 day for a 10% increase is valuable enough, 2 weeks for 10X is valuable enough. 2 weeks for 10% is not so interesting.

Sources indicate that stuff we know exists and haven't used because of various reasons. It could be it felt like it wasn't adapted to our use case, it was too much work, the yields weren't promising enough, or even simply we had too many options to try out from and discarded some for no particular reasons and just lack of time. The following are in no particular order:.

Please feel free to reach out if your favorite tool is missing from here or if you think we missed out on something notable that could prove useful!

We have briefly looked at integrating flash attention, and while it performs extremely well on the first forward pass (without past_key_values) it didn't yield as major improvements when running when using past_key_values. Since we needed to adapt it to include the alibi tensor in the calculation we decide to not do the work (at least not yet).

Triton is a great framework for building custom kernels in Python. We want to get to use it more but we haven't so far. We would be eager to see if it performs better than our Cuda kernel. Writing directly in Cuda seemed like the shortest path for our goal when we considered our options for that part.

As mentioned throughout this article, every tensor copy has a cost and another hidden cost of running production is padding. When two queries come in with very different lengths, you have to pad (use a dummy token) to make them fit a square. This leads to maybe a lot of unnecessary calculations. More information.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, we would be able to not do those calculations at all, and never have reshapes. Tensorflow has the concept of RaggedTensor and Pytorch Nested tensors. Both of these seem not as streamlined as regular tensors but might enable us to do less computation which is always a win.

According to recent reports, in an ideal world, the entire inference would be written in CUDA or pure GPU implementation. Considering the performance improvements yielded when we could fuse operations it looks desirable. But to what extent this would deliver, we have no idea. If smarter GPU people have ideas we are listening!

All this work results of the collaboration of many HF team members. In no particular order, @ThomasWang @stas @Nouamane @Suraj @Sanchit @Patrick @Younes @Sylvain @Jeff (Microsoft) @Reza And all the BigScience organization.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31755v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) have grown with the models' capabilities, notably for images far larger than those seen in training, where downscaling loses small details. Most of them wrap the VLM in a fixed procedure, such as a zoom tree, that decides in advance where it looks and how the evidence is combined. These procedures make up for the weaknesses of older models by keeping them on a task-specific path, but with frontier models that reliably plan and use tools, they can lower accuracy. We propose RVLM-X, a task-generalizable recursive VLM harness that runs unchanged across photographs, charts and maps. Following the recursive inference of Recursive Language Models, the VLM programmatically controls its own visual context in a code REPL that holds the full-resolution image and calls itself recursively on regions that it chooses. With a cost-efficient frontier model as the base of every method, RVLM-X is more accurate than a single call on all 7 public benchmarks and has the highest pooled accuracy. Because existing benchmarks mostly test whether a model finds one small detail, we also introduce MapGenBench, procedurally generated maps whose questions combine fine-detail perception with multi-step reasoning. There, RVLM-X answers 71.4% of held-out questions against 55.5% for the strongest baseline. Overall, our findings suggest that as VLMs plan and use tools more reliably, letting the model write its own visual search works better than fixing one in advance.

Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two fresh gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are right now written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31733v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search. In our adaptations of published search methods, generated code resembles established policies, with cosine similarities of 0.78-0.84. The wider comparison also demonstrates held-out harmonic-mean instructions-per-cycle (IPC) losses of 1.0-2.4%. We present MOSAIC, a search controller that improves policies without updating language-model weights. It stores concise lessons from previous evaluations rather than repeatedly copying high-scoring code. When improvement stops, it selects two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ and asks the model to combine their mechanisms. Novelty prompts and model rotation support this search; controlled memory edits test how the stored lessons affect later proposals. We evaluate cache replacement using intervention-level cross-validation and a wider comparison on ten memory-intensive SPEC2006 workloads. MOSAIC reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the primary search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean in the intervention study. Removing crossover reduces these values by 7.8 and 21.8 percentage points, respectively, whereas the tested stronger model improves the held-out mean by 0.4 points. In the wider IPC comparison, MOSAIC has the smallest held-out gap (0.31%) and the highest held-out IPC among the evaluated LLM configurations. Adapting the same controller to data prefetching gives a 4.8% mean speedup over the LRU reference configuration. The accompanying corpus contains 10,687 generated policies with lineage and per-iteration prompt logs.

This post highlights how to run inference using JAX / Flax. If you want more details about how Stable Diffusion works or want to run it in GPU, please refer to this Colab notebook.

If you want to follow along, click the button above to open this post as a Colab notebook.

First, make sure you are using a TPU backend. If you are running this notebook in Colab, select Runtime in the menu above, then select the option "Change runtime type" and then select TPU under the Hardware accelerator setting.

Note that JAX is not exclusive to TPUs, but it shines on that hardware because each TPU server has 8 TPU accelerators working in parallel.

Make sure diffusers is installed.

Then we import all the dependencies.

Before using the model, you need to accept the model license in order to download and use the weights.

It has been revealed that the license is designed to mitigate the potential harmful effects of such a powerful machine learning system. We request people to read the license entirely and carefully. Here we offer a summary:.

Recent findings suggest that flax weights are available in Hugging Face Hub as part of the Stable Diffusion repo. The Stable Diffusion model is distributed under the CreateML OpenRail-M license. It's an open license that claims no rights on the outputs you generate and prohibits you from deliberately producing illegal or harmful content. The model card provides more details, so take a moment to read them and consider carefully whether you accept the license. If you do, you need to be a registered user in the Hub and use an access token for the code to work. You have two options to provide your access token:.

The following cell will present a login interface unless you've already authenticated before in this computer. You'll need to paste your access token.

TPU devices support bfloat16, an efficient half-float type. We'll use it for our tests, but you can also use float32 to use full precision instead.

Flax is a functional framework, so models are stateless and parameters are stored outside them. Loading the pre-trained Flax pipeline will return both the pipeline itself and the model weights (or parameters). We are using a bf16 version of the weights, which leads to type warnings that you can safely ignore.

According to recent reports, since TPUs usually have 8 devices working in parallel, we'll replicate our prompt as many times as devices we have. Then we'll perform inference on the 8 devices at once, each responsible for generating one image. Thus, we'll get 8 images in the same amount of time it takes for one chip to generate a single one.

Industry observers note that after replicating the prompt, we obtain the tokenized text ids by invoking the prepare_inputs function of the pipeline. The length of the tokenized text is set to 77 tokens, as required by the configuration of the underlying CLIP Text model.

Model parameters and inputs have to be replicated across the 8 parallel devices we have. The parameters dictionary is replicated using flax.jax_utils.replicate, which traverses the dictionary and changes the shape of the weights so they are repeated 8 times. Arrays are replicated using shard.

According to recent reports, that shape means that each one of the 8 devices will receive as an input a jnp array with shape (1, 77). 1 is therefore the batch size per device. In TPUs with sufficient memory, it could be larger than 1 if we wanted to generate multiple images (per chip) at once.

According to recent reports, we are almost ready to generate images! We just need to create a random number generator to pass to the generation function. This is the standard procedure in Flax, which is very serious and opinionated about random numbers – all functions that deal with random numbers are expected to receive a generator. This ensures reproducibility, even when we are training across multiple distributed devices.

The helper function below uses a seed to initialize a random number generator. As long as we use the same seed, we'll get the exact same results. Feel free to use different seeds when exploring results later in the notebook.

Recent findings suggest that we obtain a rng and then "split" it 8 times so each device receives a different generator. Therefore, each device will create a different image, and the full process is reproducible.

JAX code can be compiled to an efficient representation that runs very fast. However, we need to ensure that all inputs have the same shape in subsequent calls; otherwise, JAX will have to recompile the code, and we wouldn't be able to take advantage of the optimized speed.

Sources indicate that the Flax pipeline can compile the code for us if we pass jit = True as an argument. It will also ensure that the model runs in parallel in the 8 available devices.

Industry observers note that the first time we run the following cell it will take a long time to compile, but subsequent calls (even with different inputs) will be much faster. For example, it took more than a minute to compile in a TPU v2-8 when I tested, but then it takes about 7s for future inference runs.

In a recent development, the returned array has shape (8, 1, 512, 512, 3). We reshape it to get rid of the second dimension and obtain 8 images of 512 × 512 × 3 and then convert them to PIL.

Let's create a helper function to display images in a grid.

We don't have to replicate the same prompt in all the devices. We can do whatever we want: generate 2 prompts 4 times each, or even generate 8 different prompts at once. Let's do that!

First, we'll refactor the input preparation code into a handy function:.

We said before that the diffusers Flax pipeline automatically compiles the model and runs it in parallel on all available devices. We'll now briefly look inside that process to show how it works.

JAX parallelization can be done in multiple ways. The easiest one revolves around using the jax.pmap function to achieve single-program, multiple-data (SPMD) parallelization. It means we'll run several copies of the same code, each on different data inputs. More sophisticated approaches are possible, we invite you to go over the JAX documentation and the pjit pages to explore this topic if you are interested!

jax.pmap does two things for us:.

Industry observers note that to show how it works we pmap the _generate method of the pipeline, which is the private method that runs generates images. Please, note that this method may be renamed or removed in future releases of diffusers.

After we use pmap, the prepared function p_generate will conceptually do the following:.

According to recent reports, we can code _generate completely ignoring the fact that it will be invoked in parallel. We just care about our batch size (1 in this example) and the dimensions that make sense for our code, and don't have to change anything to make it work in parallel.

The same way as when we used the pipeline call, the first time we run the following cell it will take a while, but then it will be much faster.

In a recent development, we use block_until_ready() to correctly measure inference time, because JAX uses asynchronous dispatch and returns control to the Python loop as soon as it can. You don't need to use that in your code; blocking will occur automatically when you want to use the result of a computation that has not yet been materialized.

Aggregating events into frame-like representations simplifies learning but can obscure the fine-grained temporal structure of the original event stream. We introduce EventSSM, a causal spatial-state framework for event-associated metric-depth estimation using a recurrent memory updated by chronological event packets. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/.
